But God's favor is not tied down to localities ( Ac 7:44 ). my people Israel-- Israel was God's people, yet He spared it not when rebellious: neither will He spare Judah, now that it rebels, though heretofore it has been His people.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9757"/><div sID="gen17245" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9757"/><hi type="bold">18. children ... fathers ... women--</hi>Not merely isolated individuals practised idolatry; young and old, men and women, and whole families, contributed their joint efforts to promote it. Oh, that there were the same zeal for the worship of God as there is for error (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.17">Jr 44:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.19.13">19:13</reference>)!<div eID="gen17245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17246" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cakes ... queen of heaven--</hi>Cakes were made of honey, fine flour, &c., in a round flat shape to resemble the disc of the moon, to which they were offered. Others read as Margin, "the frame of heaven," that is, the planets generally; so the Septuagint here; but elsewhere the Septuagint translates, "queen of heaven." The Phoenicians called the moon Ashtoreth or Astarte: the wife of Baal or Moloch, the king of heaven. The male and female pair of deities symbolized the generative powers of nature; hence arose the introduction of prostitution in the worship. The Babylonians worshipped Ashtoreth as Mylitta, that is, generative. Our Monday, or Moon-day, indicates the former prevalence of moon worship (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.65.11">Is 65:11</reference>).<div eID="gen17246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17247" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they may provoke me--</hi>implying design: in worshipping strange gods they seemed as if purposely to provoke Jehovah. <div eID="gen17247" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9761"/><div sID="gen17251" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9761"/>22. Not contradicting the divine obligation of the legal sacrifices. But, "I did not require sacrifices, unless combined with moral obedience" (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.8">Psa 50:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.16">51:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.17">17</reference>). The superior claim of the moral above the positive precepts of the law was marked by the ten commandments having been delivered first, and by the two tables of stone being deposited alone in the ark (<reference osisRef="Deut.5.6">De 5:6</reference>). The negative in Hebrew often supplies the want of the comparative: not excluding the thing denied, but only implying the prior claim of the thing set in opposition to it (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.6">Ho 6:6</reference>). "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sa 15:22</reference>). Love to God is the supreme end, external observances only means towards that end. "The mere sacrifice was not so much what I commanded, as the sincere submission to My will gives to the sacrifice all its virtue" [Magee, Atonement, Note 57]. <div eID="gen17251" type="x-p"/>
